en: The Array of Sukhāvatī [Extensive Matrix]
Oṃ, homage to the Three Jewels!
Oṃ, homage to all the glorious Buddhas and Bodhisattvas!
Homage to all the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, noble Śrāvakas, and Pratyekabuddhas, past, future, and present, who reside in the infinite and boundless world-systems of the ten directions!
Homage to Amitābha!
Homage to the one whose inner self possesses inconceivable qualities!
Thus have I heard.
At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagṛha on Vulture Peak Mountain together with a great community of monks, thirty-two thousand monks in all.

[He was surrounded] by all those Arhats who had exhausted their outflows, were free from afflictions, had dwelt [in the holy life], whose minds were well-liberated through right knowledge, whose minds were scrutinizing, whose fetters of existence were completely destroyed, who had attained their own goal, who were victorious, who had attained the supreme self-mastery, whose minds were well-liberated,

whose wisdom was well-liberated, who were great Nagas, possessed of the six superknowledges, who had attained mastery, who meditated on the eight liberations, who had attained the powers, and who were renowned for their superknowledge.
by the elder great śrāvakas,
namely: Ājñātakauṇḍinya and Aśvajit;
And with Bāṣpa,
Mahānāman, and Bhadrajit.
And by Yaśodeva, and by Vimala,
and by Subāhu;
and by Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra, and by Urubilvākāśyapa,
and by Nadīkāśyapa;
And by Gayākāśyapa, and by Kumārakāśyapa, and by Mahākāśyapa.
and with Śāriputra, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, and Mahākauṣṭhilya.
and Mahākapphiṇa, and Mahācunda, and Aniruddha,
And by Nandika, and by Kampila, and by Subhūti.
and Revata, and Khadiravanika, and Vakula,
And with Svāgata,
Amogharāja, and Pārāyaṇika;
And with Palka, Cullapalka, and Nanda.

By Rāhula, by the Venerable Ānanda, and by these and other renowned elder great śrāvakas— with the exception of one individual, namely the Venerable Ānanda, who still had duties to perform as a learner (śaikṣa)— [the assembly was gathered].
and with a great multitude of bodhisattva mahāsattvas, headed by Maitreya.
START Sukhv 2:

Then the venerable Ānanda rose from his seat, draped his upper robe over one shoulder, placed his right knee upon the ground, and bowing with palms joined toward the Blessed One, addressed the Blessed One as follows:
The faculties of the Blessed One are serene;
the color of his skin is purified, and the complexion of his face is bright and radiant with a golden luster.
Just as, for example, an autumnal lotus is pale, pure, radiant, and yellowish in luster,
even so were the Blessed One’s faculties serene and his facial complexion perfectly pure.
The color of his skin was pure, radiant with a golden luster.

Blessed One, it was just as if a coin of Jāmbūnada gold, having been cast into the mouth of a furnace by a skilled smith or a smith’s apprentice and thoroughly refined, were then placed upon a white woolen cloth; it would become exceedingly pure, perfectly bright, and radiant with a golden luster.
In the same way, the Blessed One’s faculties were serene, the color of his face was pure, and the complexion of his skin was bright and radiant with a golden luster.
Furthermore, Blessed One, I do not recall that the faculties of the Tathāgata have ever been so serene, nor his facial complexion so pure, nor his skin color so radiant and golden as it is now.
Therefore, Blessed One, this thought occurs to me: "Ah, today the Tathāgata dwells in the dwelling of a Buddha!"
"By means of the dwelling of the Victors, the dwelling of omniscience,
and the dwelling of the Great Nagas, the Tathāgata indeed dwells today;
he recollects the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Awakened Ones of the past, future, and present."
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Ānanda: "Excellent, excellent, Ānanda!
But do these deities announce this matter to you, or rather, the Buddha-Blessed Ones?"
"Then, did you know this by means of that very knowledge consisting in the investigation of the present?
When this was said, the Venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One: "No, Blessed One, the deities did not inform me of this matter, nor did the Buddha-Blessed Ones."
Nevertheless, Blessed One, by means of that very knowledge of personal investigation, it occurs to me thus: "The Tathāgata dwells today in the dwelling of a Buddha;
indeed, the Tathāgata dwells today in the dwelling of a Victor, in the dwelling of omniscience.
Or, he recollects the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, of the past, future, and present.
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Ānanda: "Excellent, excellent, Ānanda!
Truly noble is your opening of the eyes;
auspicious is your inquiry."
Excellent is your inspired eloquence!

You have set out, Ānanda, for the benefit of many, for the happiness of many, out of compassion for the world, for the sake, the welfare, and the happiness of a great multitude of beings— both gods and humans—
in that you consider the Tathāgata worthy of asking about this matter.
In the same way, Ānanda, even if one were to bring together the vision of knowledge belonging to immeasurable and incalculable Blessed Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Awakened Ones,
it would not impair the knowledge of a single Tathāgata.
Why is that?

For, Ānanda, the Tathāgata possesses unimpeded knowledge and vision regarding causes. If he so desires, Ānanda, the Tathāgata could remain for an eon on a single alms-meal, or for a hundred eons, or a hundred thousand eons, or even for hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of eons, or even longer than that.
Furthermore, the faculties of the Tathāgata would not perish,
nor would there be any change in the color of his face, nor would the complexion of his skin be impaired.
For what reason?
Because, Ānanda, the Tathāgata has attained the perfection of the gateways of meditative concentration;
and, Ānanda, the appearance of perfectly awakened ones in the world is extremely rare.
Just as the appearance of udumbara flowers in the world is extremely rare,

even so, Ānanda, the appearance of Tathāgatas— who desire the welfare of others, who seek their benefit, who are compassionate, and who are dedicated to great compassion— is extremely rare. Nevertheless, Ānanda, it is indeed through the power of the Tathāgata himself that you [have appeared] among all beings, the teachers of the world.
"Because you consider it necessary to ask the Tathāgata about this matter for the sake of the appearance in the world and for the benefit of the Bodhisattvas, the Mahāsattvas—
therefore, Ānanda, listen and pay close and careful attention."
"I shall speak to you.
"So be it, Blessed One," the venerable Ānanda replied to the Blessed One.

START Sukh-v 3: The Blessed One said this to Ānanda: "In the past, Ānanda, in a time long gone, incalculable eons ago—more than incalculable, vast, immeasurable, and inconceivable—it so happened that at that time, in that era, a Tathāgata named Dīpaṃkara, an Arhat, a perfectly awakened Buddha, appeared in the world."
Ānanda, prior to Dīpaṃkara, there was a Tathāgata named Pratāpavān; prior to him, there was a Tathāgata named Prabhākara;
and prior to him, there was a Tathāgata named Candanagandha.
After him, there was a Tathāgata named Sumerukalpa;
likewise, one named Candana,
and one named Vimalānana.
One named Anupalipta, one named Vimalaprabha,
and one named Nāgābhibhū.
named Sūryodana,
named Girirājaghoṣa, and named Merukūṭa;
One named Suvarṇaprabha,
one named Jyotiṣprabha,
and one named Vaiḍūryanirbhāsa.
named Brahmaghoṣa, named Candrābhibhū, and named Tūryaghoṣa;
The one named Muktakusumapratimaṇḍitaprabha,
the one named Śrīkūṭa,
and the one named Sāgaravarabuddhivikrīḍitābhijña.
named Varaprabha,
named Mahāgandharājanirbhāsa,
and named Vyapagatakhilamalapratighoṣa;
The one named Śūrakūṭa, the one named Raṇañjaha,
and the one named Mahāguṇadhara-buddhiprāptābhijña.
Named "The One Who Outshines the Moon and Sun," named "The One with the Radiance of Refined Vaiḍūrya," and named "The One Exalted and Fully Blossomed by the Stream of Mind and Intelligence."
The one named Saṃkusumitābhijña of the Puṣpāvatī Forest Range,
the one named Puṣpākara,
and the one named Udakacandra.
He is named the Destroyer of the Darkness of Ignorance, he is named the Lord of the World,
and he is named Like a Released Parasol in the Wind.
One named Tiṣya, one named Dharmamativinanditarāja,
and one named Siṃhasāgarajūṭavinanditarāja.
One named Sāgaramerucandra, one named Brahma-svara-nādābhinandita,
one named Kusuma-saṃbhava, and one named Prāptasena.
One named Candrabhānu, one named Candraprabha,
and one named Vimalanetra.
The one named Girirājaghoṣeśvara,
the one named Kusumaprabha,
and the one named Kusumavṛṣṭyabhiprakīrṇa.
named Ratnacandra, named Padmabimbyupaśobhita, and named Candanagandha;
One named Ratnābhibhāsa, one named Nimi, one named Mahāvyūha,
and one named Vyapagatakhiladoṣa.
Named Brahmaghoṣa,
named Saptaratnābhivṛṣṭa,
and named Mahāguṇadhara.
The one named Mahātamālapatracandanakardama, the one named Kusukābhijña,
and the one named Ajñānavidhvaṃsana.
One named Kesarī,
one named Muktacchatra,
and one named Suvarṇagarbha.
One named Vaiḍūryagarbha, one named Mahāketa, and one named Dharmaketa.
named Ratnaketu, named Ratnaśrī, and named Kolendra;
named Narendro, named Kāruṇiko, and named Lokasundara;
One named Brahmaketu, one named Dharmaketu, one named Siṃha, and one named Siṃhamati.

Ānanda, after Siṃhamati, there appeared in the world a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Lokeśvararāja— one perfected in knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, a teacher of gods and humans, a Buddha, a Blessed One.

Furthermore, Ānanda, during the teaching of that Tathāgata, Arhat, and Samyaksaṃbuddha Lokeśvararāja, there was a monk named Dharmākara who possessed supreme mindfulness, intelligence, comprehension, and wisdom;
he was supremely energetic and possessed noble resolve.

START Sukhv 4: Then indeed, Ānanda, that monk Dharmākara, rising from his seat, draped his upper robe over one shoulder, placed his right knee upon the ground, and, extending his joined palms in salutation toward where the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Lokeśvararāja, was located—
Having paid homage to the Blessed One, at that very moment he praised him to his face with these verses:
"O Buddha of infinite light, equal to the limitless! No other radiance whatsoever shines here.
The splendors of the sun, jewels, the lord of mountains, and the moon do not shine forth in all these worlds."
His form is infinite within the essence of beings, and likewise the Buddha’s voice is of infinite resonance;
in morality, concentration, wisdom, and vigor, there is no one else in this world equal to you.
The Dharma attained by the supreme Buddha is profound, vast, and subtle, like the inconceivable ocean;
therefore, there is no pride in the Teacher, and he has abandoned all faults of stubbornness for all time. (Sukhāvativyūha 3)
Then the Buddha of infinite splendor, the king of lords of men, blazes forth, illuminating all directions:
"In that way, may I become a Buddha, a Lord of Dharma, and liberate all beings from old age and death. (Sukhāvativyūha 4)

Through generosity, tranquility, ethical discipline, patience, vigor, meditation, and concentration—the most supreme and excellent—I undertake these vows: "May I become a Buddha, a savior of all sentient beings. (Sukhāvativyūha 5)
Seeking the peerless, auspicious, and supreme enlightenment, I shall worship hundreds of thousands of kotis of Buddhas— limitless as the sands of the Ganges— in every way.
In those worlds, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, and even further into infinite realms beyond, I shall emit light everywhere; such vigor should one exert.
This field of mine is vast, supreme, and most excellent; here, in this purified realm,
there is the incomparable bliss of the sphere of nirvāṇa.
I shall purify it by means of its non-existence as a sentient being.
Beings gathered from the ten directions who have come there quickly grant me happiness;
may the Buddha be my witness here as I train myself and generate the aspiration for the power of unerring diligence. (Sukhāvativyūha 9)
May those who possess unimpeded knowledge of the worlds in the ten directions always know my mind;
even if I must go to the Avīci hell, may I dwell there forever, for I shall never turn back from the power of my vow.
START Sukhv 5: (Sukhv,
Vaidya 225) Then, Ānanda, that monk Dharmākara, having praised the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Lokeśvararāja, face-to-face with these verses—

He said this: "Blessed One, I am desirous of awakening to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Again and again I generate the mind set on unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment and I dedicate it.
May the Blessed One, my teacher, teach me the Dharma accordingly."
"May I swiftly awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment;
may I become an Asamasama Tathāgata in the world.
And may the Blessed One proclaim those qualities by which I may acquire the excellence of the array of virtues of a Buddha-field."

When this had been said, Ānanda, the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Lokeśvararāja, spoke thus to that bhikṣu: "In that case, bhikṣu, you yourself should take hold of the perfection of the array of the ornaments and qualities of a buddha-field.
He replied: "I would not be able to do that, Blessed One."
Rather, may the Blessed One himself speak of the excellence of the array of qualities and the adornments of the buddha-fields of other Tathāgatas,
hearing which we shall fulfill them in every aspect.

Then, Ānanda, that Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Lokeśvararāja, having understood the intention of that monk, out of desire for their welfare, seeking their benefit, and out of compassion, having taken up compassion, for a full ten million years revealed— complete with its forms, its details, and its explanations— the perfect excellence of the array of qualities and ornaments of the buddha-fields of eighty-one hundred thousand times ten million buddhas.
Having generated great compassion for sentient beings so that the Buddha-fields would not be interrupted,
the lifespan of that Blessed One, the Tathāgata, was forty full eons.
START Sukhv 6: (Sukhv,

Vaidya 226) Then indeed, Ānanda, that monk Dharmākara [took] those eighty-one hundred thousand nayutas of kotis of Buddhas’ perfections of the arrays of the qualities and ornaments of their Buddha-fields.

Having gathered all of them into a single buddha-field, he bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Lokeśvararāja, circumambulated him, and departed from the presence of that Blessed One. Furthermore, for five kalpas, he took possession of a perfection of the array of ornaments and qualities of a buddha-field that was more exalted and more sublime than any previously known in all the worlds of the ten directions, and he made a most exalted vow.

START Sukh-v 7: Thus indeed, Ānanda, having taken up a buddha-field endowment eighty-one times more magnificent, sublime, and immeasurable than the endowment of those eighty-one hundred thousand million billion buddha-fields described by that Blessed One, the Tathāgata Lokeśvararāja, the monk [proceeded] where—

He approached that Tathāgata, bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, and said this: "Blessed One, I have fully grasped the excellence of the array of the ornaments and qualities of the Buddha-field.
When this had been said, Ānanda, that Tathāgata Lokeśvararāja said to that bhikṣu: "In that case, bhikṣu, speak!"
The Tathāgata approves;
this is the time, O Bhikṣu,
gladden the assembly.
Produce joy and roar the lion’s roar,
hearing which the bodhisattva mahāsattvas of the present and the future will take up such stations for their vows regarding the excellence of the qualities of a buddha-field.

Then, Ānanda, at that time, the bhikṣu Dharmākara said this to the Blessed One: "Therefore, may the Blessed One listen to me regarding my specific vows, so that when I have awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, that buddha-field shall be endowed with an array of inconceivable qualities and ornaments."

START Sukhv 8: 1. O Blessed One, if in that buddha-field there should be hell, or the animal realm, or the domain of hungry ghosts, or the host of asuras, may I never awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
2. "O Blessed One, if those beings who have been reborn in that Buddha-field of mine were,
upon passing away from there, to fall again into hell, or into the animal realm, or into the domain of hungry ghosts, or into the body of an asura,
may I not then awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."

3. "O Bhagavān, if in that buddha-field all the beings who are reborn there were not of a single color—namely, of golden color—then may I not awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."

4. "O Blessed One, if in that buddha-field any distinction between gods and humans were perceived, other than as a mere conventional designation and worldly usage in terms of calculation and enumeration—such as the numbers 'gods' and 'humans'—may I not attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening."

5. "O Blessed One, if all those beings who have been reborn in that buddha-field were not to have attained supreme perfection in mastery over supernatural powers— even to the extent of traversing hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of buddha-fields in a single moment of thought, "O Blessed One, if all those beings who have been reborn in that buddha-field were not to have attained supreme perfection in mastery over supernatural powers— even to the extent of traversing hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of buddha-fields in a single moment of thought, I would not attain perfect awakening."
May I not, for that long, realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening.

6. "O Blessed One, if all those beings who are reborn in that buddha-field should not be rememberers of their past lives— even to the extent of recollecting hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of eons— then may I not attain perfect awakening."
May I not, for that long, fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

7. "If, Blessed One, those beings who would be reborn in that buddha-field were all not to obtain the divine eye, even to the extent of seeing hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of world-systems; [may I not attain perfect enlightenment]."
May I not awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment until then.

8. "If, Blessed One, those beings who are born in that buddha-field should all not become possessors of the divine ear, such that they might simultaneously hear the true Dharma even from as far as hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of buddha-fields; [then may I not attain perfect awakening]."
May I not, for that long, awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

9. "O Blessed One, if all those beings who are reborn in that buddha-field were not experts in knowing the minds of others— even to the extent of fully understanding the mental conduct of beings included within hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of buddha-fields— then may I not attain perfect awakening."
May I not, for that long, fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

10. "If, Blessed One, when those beings are reborn in that buddha-field, the notion of possession should arise in them— even with regard to their own bodies— [may I not attain perfect enlightenment]."
May I not, for that long, awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

11. "O Blessed One, if those beings who are reborn in that buddha-field were not all destined for rightness, up to and including great parinirvāṇa, may I not awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
12. "O Blessed One, if, when I have awakened to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment in that buddha-field, any sentient being were to reach the calculation of the assembly of śrāvakas—
even if all sentient beings included within the triple-thousand great thousandfold world-system were to become pratyekabuddhas and calculate for hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of eons—
may I not then awaken to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment."

13. "O Blessed One, if, when I have awakened to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment in that buddha-field, my radiance should be limited— even by the measure of hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of buddha-fields—
then may I not awaken to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment."

(Śukhāv, Vaidya 227) 14. "O Blessed One, if, when I have awakened to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment, the lifespan of the beings in that buddha-field should be fixed in measure— except by the power of their own vows— then may I not attain perfect enlightenment."
May I not, for that long, fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

15. Blessed One, if, when I have attained awakening, my lifespan were to have a limit— even if it were to be counted by hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of eons— may I not then realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening.

16. "O Blessed One, if, when I have attained awakening, there should be even the name of 'unwholesome' among the beings in that buddha-field, may I not then awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."

17. "If, O Blessed One, when I have attained awakening, immeasurable and incalculable Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, in immeasurable Buddha-fields were not to proclaim my name, nor speak my praise, nor utter my commendation; [then may I not attain perfect awakening]."
If they should not proclaim it,
may I not first awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

18. "Blessed One, if, when I have attained enlightenment, there should be beings in other world-systems who, having resolved their minds upon unsurpassed perfect enlightenment, hear my name and develop a serene mind, yet at the time of their death— when it has arrived— I do not stand before them, surrounded and honored by the community of monks, for the sake of ensuring their minds are undistracted, then may I not attain unsurpassed perfect enlightenment."

19. "O Blessed One, if, when I have attained awakening, those beings in immeasurable and incalculable Buddha-fields who, having heard my name, should direct their minds toward that Buddha-field and dedicate their roots of merit for the sake of rebirth there, were not to be reborn in that Buddha-field, [then may I not attain perfect awakening]."

Even if it takes ten cycles of generating the thought of enlightenment, I shall not attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening— unless, that is, there are beings who have committed the immediate transgressions or who have created the obstruction of rejecting the true Dharma.

20. "O Blessed One, may it be so that when I have attained awakening, whatever beings are reborn in that buddha-field shall all be bound to only one more birth before attaining unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening— except for those who have made specific vows— and may they be bodhisattvas, mahāsattvas, girded with the great armor, awakened for the sake of the entire world."

Of those who are dedicated to the welfare of all worlds, who are dedicated to the parinirvāṇa of all worlds, who desire to practice the conduct of a bodhisattva in all world-systems, who desire to bring about the manifestation of all Buddhas, who establish beings as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā in unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, and who furthermore are oriented toward the higher conduct and have emerged from the conduct of Samantabhadra.
May I not, for that long, fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

21. "If, O Blessed One, when I have attained awakening, those bodhisattvas who are born in that buddha-field should all, in a single morning meal, go to other buddha-fields and [behold] many hundreds of Buddhas, many thousands of Buddhas,
many hundreds of thousands of Buddhas, many millions of Buddhas, up to many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddhas."
If they were not to be attended by all the requisites for happiness through the power of the Buddhas,
then may I not attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening.

22. "O Bhagavat, may it be so that when I have attained awakening in that buddha-field, the bodhisattvas there may, according to their respective desires, plant roots of merit by means of gold or silver, or by means of gems, pearls, lapis lazuli, conch shells, crystals, coral, rock crystal, musāragalva, red pearls, emeralds, and so forth;
or by any one or all of the various jewels; or by any of the perfumes, flowers, garlands, ointments, incense, powders, robes, parasols, banners, flags, or lamps."
Or, if through all manner of dance, song, and instrumental music,
as well as their corresponding types of food, these things were not to appear simultaneously with the arising of their thought,
may I not attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening.
23. "O Blessed One, if, when I have attained awakening, those beings who are born in that buddha-field should all not speak discourses on the Dharma accompanied by omniscience,
may I not then awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening."
24. "If, O Blessed One, when I have attained enlightenment, those bodhisattvas in that buddha-field should conceive such a thought as this:

'Remaining right here in this world-system, may we honor, revere, respect, and worship the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, in immeasurable and incalculable buddha-fields—namely, with robes, alms-food, bedding and seats, and medicinal requisites for the sick.'"

With flowers, incense, lamps, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, parasols, banners, and flags; with various kinds of dances, songs, and instrumental music; and with rains of jewels—if those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, should not accept these out of compassion at the very moment my thought [of awakening] arises, then may I not awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

25. "O Blessed One, if, when I have attained enlightenment, those bodhisattvas who are born in that buddha-field were not all to obtain a physical body as firm and powerful as Nārāyaṇa and as indestructible as a diamond,
may I not then awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."

26. "O Blessed One, may it be that when I have attained awakening, if any sentient being in that buddha-field were to grasp the limit of the description of its ornaments—even with a divine eye—such that they would know this buddha-field to be of such color and such splendor, yet perceive it as having various colors; [may this not be so]."
May I not, for that long, awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

27. "O Blessed One, if, when I have attained enlightenment, any bodhisattva in that buddha-field who possesses even the most meager roots of merit should not perceive the Bodhi tree— of magnificent color and rising to at least one hundred yojanas—
may I not then awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
28. "O Blessed One, if, when I have attained enlightenment, there should be any sentient being in that Buddha-field who must perform either formal instruction or recitation,
and they were not all to attain the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), may I not awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."

29. "Blessed One, if, when I have attained awakening, that Buddha-field of mine were not so luminous that from all sides immeasurable, incalculable, inconceivable, incomparable, and limitless Buddha-fields would be visible—just as, for example, the reflection of a face appears in a well-polished mirror-surface; [then may I not attain perfect awakening]."
May I not, for that long, fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

30. "O Bhagavat, may it be that when I have attained enlightenment, in that buddha-field—from the surface of the earth up to the sky—there shall always be hundreds of thousands of various fragrant incense burners made of all kinds of jewels, emitting noble incense that transcends the range of gods and humans, and which is worthy of being offered to the Tathāgata and the Bodhisattvas; if this should not be so, [may I not attain perfect enlightenment]."
May I not awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment until then.
