There are lotuses there measuring half a yojana, some measuring one yojana, and some measuring two, three, four, or five yojanas.
They extend for as much as ten *yojanas* in measure.
From every jewel-lotus, three million six hundred thousand rays of light stream forth.
And from every opening of those rays, three million six hundred thousand Buddhas emerge, with bodies of golden hue, bearing the thirty-two marks of a Great Man.

Having gone to immeasurable and incalculable world-systems in the eastern direction, they teach the Dharma to sentient beings. Likewise, having gone to immeasurable and incalculable world-systems in the southern, western, and northern directions, below, above, and in the intermediate directions— having traversed the unobstructed world— they teach the Dharma to sentient beings.
Furthermore, Ānanda, in that buddha-field there are no mountains of iron at all; rather, there are entirely mountains of jewels, including all the Sumerus, kings of mountains,
and all the Cakravālas and Mahācakravālas, kings of mountains.
And all around that buddha-field, it was level, delightful, like the palm of a hand, with its ground strewn with various kinds of jewels and gems.

When this had been said, the venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One: "But, Blessed One, as for those gods of the Four Great Kings who dwell on the slopes of Sumeru, or the Trāyastriṃśa gods on the summit of Sumeru, where are they situated?"

The Blessed One said: "What do you think, Ānanda? As for those Yāma gods, Tuṣita gods, Nirmāṇarati gods, Paranirmitavaśavartin gods, Brahmakāyika gods, Brahmapurohita gods, Mahābrahmāṇas, up to the Akaniṣṭha gods who are here upon Sumeru, the king of mountains—"
"Where are they established?
Ānanda said, "Lord, the ripening of actions and the formation of actions are inconceivable.

The Blessed One said, "Ānanda, you have understood here that the ripening of actions and the formation of actions are inconceivable; however, the inconceivable buddha-empowerment of the Blessed Buddhas who have performed meritorious deeds is not [within your grasp]."
"And for those beings who have planted roots of merit, your inconceivable manifestation of merit is [unfathomable].
Ānanda said: "O Blessed One, I have no hesitation, nor doubt, nor uncertainty regarding this."
"Nevertheless, I ask the Tathāgata about this matter for the sake of destroying the doubts, hesitations, and uncertainties of future beings.
The Blessed One said, "Excellent, excellent, Ānanda! You should act in this way."
START Sukhv 18: Indeed, Ānanda, in that world-system Sukhāvatī, various kinds of rivers flow.
There are great rivers there that are one *yojana* in width.

There are rivers extending twenty, thirty, forty, and fifty yojanas in width, and reaching even twelve yojanas in depth. All those rivers flow pleasantly, carrying waters fragrant with various perfumes, bearing clusters of flowers mixed with various jewels, and resounding with the sounds of various sweet melodies.
And, Ānanda, [there is the sound] of musical instruments accompanied by hundreds of thousands of millions of limbs, blended with divine songs.
When played upon by those skilled [musicians], a delightful sound issues forth; such is the resonance that issues from those great rivers—
profound, unknowable, incomprehensible, flawless, pleasant to the ear, heart-stirring, lovely, charming,
enchanting, agreeable, and not discordant to hear.
"Impermanent, peaceful, and selfless"— these words, so pleasant to hear, reach the range of the auditory faculties of those beings.
Furthermore, Ānanda, both banks of those great rivers are covered with various trees of fragrant jewels,
from which various branches, leaves, flowers, and clusters of blossoms hang down.

There, those beings who desire to experience divine, delightful, and charming pleasures and amusements on those riverbanks find that when they have entered the rivers with such desires, the water stands only at their ankles;
for those who so desire, it stands only at their knees, their waists, or their armpits.
For those who desire it, water remains at the mere depth of the ear,
and divine delights manifest;
therein, those beings who wish for cool water, [it becomes so].
For them, the water becomes cool;
for those who desire it to become warm, it becomes warm for them.
For those who desire it to be cold or warm, that water becomes cold or warm according to their pleasure;
and those great rivers are filled with water perfumed by the exquisite scents of celestial *tamāla* leaves, *agaru*, *kālānusārin*, *tagara*, and the finest *uragasāra* sandalwood.

They flow along, covered with divine flowers such as utpalas, padmas, kumudas, puṇḍarīkas, and saugandhikas; their sandy banks are frequented by throngs of birds emanated by the Tathāgata—such as swans, cranes, curlews, ruddy geese, kāraṇḍavas, parrots, mynas, cuckoos, kuṇālas, kalaviṅkas, and peacocks—possessing delightful voices; they are graced by *dhārtarāṣṭra* geese, have excellent landing-stairs, are free from mud, and are strewn with golden sand.
In that regard, whenever those beings desire, "May our intentions be fulfilled in such a way," then their very intentions are fulfilled accordingly.
And that sound of the water, Ānanda, which issues forth as delightful, makes itself known throughout that entire buddha-field;
yet those beings standing on the riverbanks who wish, "May this sound not come within the range of our sense of hearing," [do not hear it].
Even for them, it does not come within the range of their divine faculty of hearing;
yet, whoever desires to hear a sound of such a kind as they wish, they hear that very same kind of pleasant sound.

Namely: the sound of "Buddha," the sound of "Dharma," the sound of "Saṅgha," the sound of the "perfections" (pāramitā), the sound of the "stages" (bhūmi), the sound of the "powers" (bala), the sound of the "fearlessnesses" (vaiśāradya), the sound of the "unique qualities of a Buddha" (āveṇikabuddhadharma), the sound of the "analytical knowledges" (pratisaṃvid), the sound of emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, lack of formative activity, non-arising, non-origination, non-existence, and cessation;

the sound of peace, perfect peace, and total tranquility; the sound of great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity; and the sound of the attainment of the stage of consecration through the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattikadharmakṣānti).

Having heard it, one attains noble joy and gladness accompanied by seclusion, accompanied by dispassion, accompanied by peace, accompanied by cessation, accompanied by the Dharma, and accompanied by the roots of merit for the perfect accomplishment of awakening.
Furthermore, Ānanda, in the world-system Sukhāvatī, the word "unwholesome" does not exist in any way whatsoever.
Everywhere there is no sound of hindrances; everywhere there is no sound of the states of woe, miserable destinies, or downfall; everywhere there is no sound of suffering.
Even the word "neither-painful-nor-pleasant-feeling" does not exist there, Ānanda; how much less could there be the word "suffering"?
Therefore, Ānanda, it is for this reason that, in brief, that world-system is called Sukhāvatī.
Furthermore, Ānanda, even if an eon were to come to an end while the causes of happiness in the world-system Sukhāvatī were being described in detail,
it would still not be possible to reach the limit of those causes of happiness.
Furthermore, Ānanda, all those beings who have been born, are being born, or will be born in that world-system Sukhāvatī,
they are all alike in their complexion, strength, power, stature, circumference, sovereignty, and accumulation of merit.

They were endowed with the enjoyment of garments, ornaments, gardens, palaces, and gabled chambers that were not too hot, as well as with such enjoyments of sounds, smells, tastes, and tangibles, and indeed with all such varieties of wealth and luxury, just like the gods who wield power over the creations of others (Paranirmitavaśavartin).
Furthermore, Ānanda, the beings in the world-system Sukhāvatī do not consume food in the form of coarse broth or molasses; rather, whatever kind of food they desire,
that very kind of food they perceive as having been consumed.
Their bodies become refreshed and their minds are gladdened;
no further application [of ointments] needs to be made to their bodies.
With their bodies thus refreshed, they desire such varieties of fragrances that by those very same divine fragrances, that entire buddha-field becomes completely perfumed.
In that regard, for whoever desires to smell that fragrance, no latent predisposition (*vāsanā*) toward being a king of the *gandharvas* arises in them at all.
Likewise, for those who desire various kinds of perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, parasols, banners, flags, and musical instruments, [no such predispositions arise].
By those such robes of theirs, that entire buddha-field becomes completely filled. If they desire robes of various colors— many hundreds of thousands of colors—
that entire buddha-field becomes completely filled with such very same precious robes.
They perceive themselves as being clothed;
they desire ornaments of various kinds,
such as head-ornaments, ear-ornaments, neck-ornaments, or ornaments for the hands and feet.

Or rather, these are the crowns, earrings, bracelets, armlets, pearl necklaces, gold chains, pendants, signet rings, golden threads, girdles, golden filigree, nets of pearls, nets of all kinds of jewels, and nets of golden-jeweled bells; with such ornaments, inlaid with hundreds of thousands of various gems, [the land] is resplendent.
They behold that buddha-field, which is adorned with those ornaments suspended from the trees of jewelry;
they perceive themselves as being likewise adorned by those ornaments.

Whatever kind of celestial palace (vimāna) they desire—whatever its color, mark, and shape, and its height and circumference—adorned with hundreds of thousands of turrets made of various jewels and strewn with various divine flowers, [they see it].
A celestial palace exactly like that appears before them;
in those palaces produced by their own minds, they dwell, surrounded and honored by seven thousand apsarases each, playing, sporting, enjoying themselves, and taking their pleasure.
START Sukh-v 20:
And in that world-system there is no diversity among gods or humans, except that by way of conventional usage they are designated as "gods" and "humans.
Ānanda, it is just as, for example, before a universal monarch (cakravartin), a wretched human, a mere semblance of a man, does not shine, does not glow, and does not radiate.

And he is neither confident nor radiant; even so, in the presence of the gods of the Heaven of Controlling Others' Emanations (Paranirmitavaśavartin), Śakra, the lord of the gods, does not shine, does not glow, and does not radiate— whether by means of his gardens, celestial palaces, garments, ornaments, sovereignty, supernatural power, or miraculous displays.
Or by sovereignty, Ānanda; indeed, it is through the realization of the Dharma or the enjoyment of the Dharma.
In this regard, Ānanda, it is like the gods who wield power over the emanations of others (paranirmitavaśavartin).
In this way, the humans in the world-system of Sukhāvatī are to be regarded. // Sukhv_20 //
Furthermore, Ānanda, when the forenoon has arrived in that world-system Sukhāvatī, winds blow from all four directions— turbulent and swirling—
which cause those jewel-trees to display various beautiful forms of many colors and many stalks, perfumed by various divine fragrances of exquisite scent.

They stir, they cause great agitation, they move, and they cause movement, so that many hundreds of flowers— possessing delightful fragrances and beautiful to behold— fall upon that great earth made of jewels; and by those flowers, that buddha-field becomes adorned for seven fathoms on all sides with a refined appearance.
It was just as if a man skilled in the art of the earth were to spread out a carpet of flowers, arranging it evenly with both hands so that it was most variegated and beautiful to behold;
even so, that buddha-field was completely covered for seven fathoms on all sides by those flowers of various scents and colors.

And those varieties of flowers were soft, with a pleasant touch like that of kācilindika cloth; they were merely by way of comparison such that when a foot was set down, they sank four finger-breadths,
and when the foot was lifted, they rose up exactly four finger-breadths.
When the forenoon has passed, those flowers disappear without remainder;
then that buddha-field becomes secluded, delightful, and pure, free from the previous flowers.
Thereupon, winds blow again from all four directions.
Those who scatter fresh flowers as before—
at the time of the forenoon, likewise at the time of midday, at twilight, and during the first, middle, and last watches of the night— [attain these fruits].

When those beings are touched by those winds, which blow, perfumed with various fragrances, they become so endowed with bliss that it is just like a monk who has entered the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpanna*).
Furthermore, Ānanda, in that buddha-field, there is not even the mention or the conceptual designation of fire, sun, moon, planets, constellations, stars, or forms of darkness.
In every respect, throughout day and night, there is not even the designation [of "mine"], except for the conventional usage of the Tathāgata;
and in every respect, there is no perception of possession regarding gardens.
Furthermore, Ānanda, at that time in that world-system Sukhāvatī, clouds of divine fragrant water rain down, as well as divine flowers of every color and divine seven-jeweled gems.
They rained down divine sandalwood powder, divine parasols, banners, and flags,
and divine flowers of every color.
Divine canopies are held aloft,
and divine jewel-umbrellas along with all kinds of ornaments are suspended in the sky.
Divine musical instruments resound,
and divine apsarases dance.
Furthermore, Ānanda, all those beings who have been born, are being born, or will be born in that buddha-field are fixed in rightness until they reach nirvāṇa.
For what reason?
Because there is no establishment or designation of two groups therein, namely, those who are indefinite or those who are fixed in falsehood.
Therefore, Ānanda, by this method as well, that world-system is called Sukhāvatī in brief.
But it would not be told in detail;
even if, Ānanda, an entire eon were exhausted while the causes of happiness in the world-system Sukhāvatī were being proclaimed,
it would still be impossible to reach the end of those causes of happiness.
START Sukhv 25:
Then, at that time, the Blessed One spoke these verses:
"May all sentient beings be happy, possessing pure knowledge and skilled in the ultimate truth."
They might then proclaim the description of Sukhāvatī for ten million eons or even longer.
Even at the end of ten million eons, O Vajra, the gods in Sukhāvatī do not reach the limit of its beauty;
nor does their eloquence ever come to an end as they proclaim its manifold virtues.

If one were to divide and break apart world-systems as numerous as atoms and turn them into dust, and then fill even more world-systems than those with jewels and give them away as a gift; [Sukhāvya-vyūha 25]

Even a fraction or even a mere comparison of that merit would not suffice for all the vast world-systems; yet such is the merit that arises here simply by hearing the name of the world-system Sukhāvatī. (Sukhāvatīvyūha 26)
Then there would be great merit for those who, possessing wisdom, have faith in the word of the Jina;
for faith is the root for attaining the world [of liberation]. Therefore, having heard it, one should dispel doubt through investigation. (Sukhāvativyūha 27)
Thus it is said.
Thus, Ānanda, the world-system Sukhāvatī possesses such immeasurable qualities and praises.
Furthermore, Ānanda, in each of the ten directions,

in as many Buddha-fields as there are grains of sand in the river Gaṅgā, there are Buddhas, Blessed Ones, equal in number to the grains of sand in the river Gaṅgā, who proclaim the name of that Blessed One, the Tathāgata Amitābha.
They proclaim them, speak their praises,
and manifest their glory.
They proclaim his virtues.
For what reason?
Because whatever beings hear the name of that Blessed One Amitābha, [they shall all attain supreme enlightenment].

And having heard [this], even if they generate but a single thought with a resolute intention accompanied by serene faith, they all become irreversible from unexcelled, perfect enlightenment. (Sukhāvativyūha 26)
START Sukhv 27:
And furthermore, Ānanda, whatever beings shall again bring that Tathāgata to mind with reverence,
and shall plant a vast and immeasurable root of merit by dedicating their minds toward awakening—
And they shall make a vow for rebirth in that world-system;
when the time of death has arrived for them, that Tathāgata Amitābha, the Arhat, the Perfectly Awakened One, surrounded and honored by a multitude of many monks, will stand before them.
Then, having seen that Blessed One with a serene mind, they, upon passing away, will be reborn right there in the world-system Sukhāvatī.
And whoever, Ānanda, be it a son of good family or a daughter of good family, should desire: "How might I see that Tathāgata Amitābha in this very life?"— by them,

having generated the mind set on unsurpassed perfect enlightenment, with a continuity of superior resolve and by directing the mind toward that buddha-field for the sake of rebirth there, they should dedicate their roots of merit.
Furthermore, for those who will no longer bring that Tathāgata to mind, nor repeatedly plant abundant and immeasurable roots of merit,

for them that Tathāgata Amitābha— the Arhat, the Perfectly Awakened One— will appear as a mental creation with exactly such color, shape, height, and girth, and with a retinue of a monastic community exactly like his own.
At the time of death, he will stand before them.

By means of that very samādhi which takes as its object the serene faith from seeing the Tathāgata, and with mindfulness undiminished, they will pass away and be reborn in that very same buddha-field.
START Sukhv 29:
Furthermore, Ānanda, those beings who shall recollect that Tathāgata for ten moments of thought and shall conceive a longing for that Buddha-field,
When profound dharmas are being taught, they will attain satisfaction;
they will not be distressed, nor will they fall into despair.
They will not fall into despair;
even with the production of a single thought, they will bring that Tathāgata to mind and will conceive a longing for that buddha-field.
They too, having entered into a dream, will behold the Tathāgata Amitābha; they will be reborn in the world-system of Sukhāvatī,
and they will become non-retrogressive regarding unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
START Sukhv 30: Indeed, Ānanda, seeing this very purpose, the Tathāgatas in the ten directions, throughout immeasurable and incalculable world-systems,
proclaim the name of that Tathāgata Amitābha, utter his praise, and raise up his eulogy.

Furthermore, Ānanda, in that buddha-field, from each of the ten directions, bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā approach that Tathāgata Amitābha to see him, to pay homage to him, to attend upon him, and to question him;
they do so to behold that assembly of bodhisattvas and those extraordinary perfections of the array of qualities and ornaments of that buddha-field.
START Sukhv 31:
Then, at that time, the Blessed One, wishing to illuminate this very matter more extensively, spoke these verses:
"Just as there are Buddha-fields equal in number to the sands of the river Ganges, so too is the field of the Leader Amitāyus. Sukhv_vs_28 //

Taking many flower-baskets of various colors, fragrant and delightful, they scatter them over Amitāyus, the supreme leader of men, who is honored by gods and humans. (Sukhv, Vaidya 242) Sukhv_vs_29 //
Likewise, from as many Buddha-fields as there are in the south, west, north, and the ten directions,
they come from wherever they may be to pay homage to the Buddha Amitāyus, together with the bodhisattvas.
Taking many small bags of incense— of various colors, fragrant, and delightful—
they scatter them over Amitāyus, the supreme leader of men, who is honored by gods and humans.
Having honored those many bodhisattvas and having bowed at the feet of Amitaprabha, they circumambulated him and spoke thus: "Oh, how wonderful! This buddha-field shines with such splendor!"
With uplifted minds and incomparable joy, they scatter handfuls of flowers once more and speak before the Leader: "May our field also become like this! (Sukhāvativyūha 33)
The flower-baskets that were thrown there remained suspended as a parasol for a hundred yojanas;
beautifully adorned and radiating diverse splendors, it covered the entire body of the Buddha.
Having thus honored them, those bodhisattvas act with such joy therein that those beings who have heard the name of the Supreme among Men have indeed gained a great gain. (Sukhāvativyūha 35)
We too have previously obtained great gain when we came to this buddha-field;
behold how such a dream-like state of loving-kindness was fashioned for the Teacher throughout a thousand eons.
Behold the Buddha, that supreme mass of merit, resplendent as he is surrounded by bodhisattvas;
Amitābha’s light is immeasurable, his splendor is immeasurable, his lifespan is immeasurable, and his Saṅgha is immeasurable.
The Lord Amitāyus smiles, emitting thirty-six quintillion rays of light from his countenance,
which radiate forth and pervade thousands of millions of buddha-fields.
Having returned there once more, those all-surpassing rays reach the summit at the time of the Leader’s parinirvāṇa;
then, gods and humans experience joy, perceiving that this radiance has come to an end.
The son of the Buddha of great renown has arisen; he is indeed the Lord Avalokiteśvara.
What is the cause here, O Blessed One, what is the reason that you, the Protector of the World, manifest a smile? (Sukhāvativyūha 40)
"Prophesy concerning him, that expert in meaning, who is compassionate for the welfare of others and the liberator of many beings;
having heard these most excellent and delightful words, sentient beings will become uplifted in heart. (Sukhāvativyūha 41)
Those Bodhisattvas who, setting out from many world-systems for Sukhāvatī, behold the Buddha—
hearing this, let them give rise to vast joy and quickly behold this field.
And having come to this sublime field, they quickly attained the power of supernatural faculties;
they possessed divine sight and likewise divine hearing, remembered their past births, and were masters of the perfections.
Then the Buddha Amitāyus granted me this prophecy: "In the past, such was my vow:
'By whatever means possible, may sentient beings, upon hearing my name, always go to my land. (Sukhāvativyūha 44)
This beautiful vow of mine has been fulfilled; and these beings from many world-systems,
having come quickly into my presence, become non-retrogressive and destined for only one more birth here.
Therefore, whatever bodhisattva here desires, "May my field also be of such a kind;
may I too liberate many beings by means of my name, my voice, and my sight," [should cultivate this practice].
May he go very swiftly, in a state of great haste, to the world-system Sukhāvatī;
and having gone there, may he first worship ten million billion Buddhas of Infinite Light.
Having honored many millions of Buddhas and traveled to many fields by the power of their supernatural faculties,
they will perform worship in the presence of the Sugatas and, out of devotion, go from there to Sukhāvatī.
Thus [it is said]. (Sukhāvativyūha 31)
Furthermore, Ānanda, the Bodhi tree of that Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Amitāyus is one thousand yojanas in height.

Its branches, leaves, and foliage extend for eight hundred *yojanas*; its roots measure five hundred *yojanas* in height and circumference; it is always in leaf, always in flower, and always in fruit; it possesses various colors and many hundreds of thousands of colors;

it has various leaves, various flowers, and various fruits; it is adorned with various wonderful ornaments; it is clearly illuminated by moon-like radiant *maṇi*-jewels; it is variegated with *maṇi*-jewels fixed by Śakra; and it is strewn with *cintāmaṇi* jewels.

It was exquisitely adorned with the finest jewels from the ocean, surpassing all that is divine; it was draped with golden threads and decorated with clusters of *rucaka* necklaces, pearl necklaces, jewel necklaces, *vatsa* necklaces, bracelets, *kaṭaka* bracelets, necklaces of red pearls, necklaces of blue pearls, *siṃhalatā* girdles, waist-bands, jeweled cords, and hundreds of various precious objects.

It was further embellished with nets of gold, nets of pearls, nets of all kinds of jewels, and nets of tiny bells, and was beautifully ornamented with *makara* motifs, svastikas, *nandyāvarta* designs, and moons.

It was adorned with ornaments of all kinds of jewels, including nets of bells and jewels and golden decorations; furthermore, it was beautifully embellished according to the mental inclinations and perceptions of sentient beings.

Moreover, Ānanda, when that Bodhi tree is stirred by the wind, the sound and resonance that issues forth makes itself known throughout immeasurable world-systems. In that regard, Ānanda, for those sentient beings to whose ears that Bodhi tree comes as an auditory perception, [it brings about their benefit].
For them, no disease of the ear is to be expected until the end of awakening.
For those immeasurable, incalculable, inconceivable, incomparable, unfathomable, limitless, and inexpressible beings to whom that Bodhi tree comes into the range of vision,
no disease of the eye is to be expected until the end of awakening.
Furthermore, Ānanda, those beings who smell the fragrance from that Bodhi tree—
for them, until they reach the limit of enlightenment, the disease of the nose shall never be expected. Those beings who taste the fruits from that Bodhi tree—
For them, until the limit of enlightenment, no disease of the tongue should ever be expected.
Those beings who are pervaded by the radiance of that Bodhi-tree—
for them, until the limit of enlightenment, no disease of the body should ever be expected.
Furthermore, Ānanda, as for those beings who contemplate that Bodhi tree according to the Dharma,

from that moment until they reach the limit of enlightenment, no distraction of mind should ever be expected of them. And all those beings, upon merely seeing that Bodhi tree, become irreversible from unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
And they attain three kinds of receptivities— namely, the receptivity that follows the sound, the conformable receptivity, and the receptivity to the non-arising of phenomena—
by virtue of the empowerment of the former vows of that very Tathāgata Amitāyus, through their prior service to former Victors,
and by having perfectly completed and well-cultivated their former vows without deficiency or omission.

Furthermore, Ānanda, all those bodhisattvas who have been born, are being born, or will be born right there are bound by only one more birth; they shall all realize unexcelled, perfect enlightenment from that very state, with the exception of...
Those Bodhisattvas who, by the power of their vows, utter the great lion’s roar, are clad in the armor of noble resolve, and are dedicated to bringing all sentient beings to final nirvana.

Furthermore, Ānanda, in that buddha-field, those who are śrāvakas there possess a radiance of one fathom, whereas those who are bodhisattvas possess a radiance of hundreds of thousands of millions of yojanas.
Except for two bodhisattvas, by whose radiance that world-system is constantly and perpetually suffused with light.
Then the Venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, what are the names of those two bodhisattva mahāsattvas?
The Blessed One replied: "Ānanda, one of them is the bodhisattva mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, and the second is named Mahāsthāmaprāpta."
And from this very Buddha-field, Ānanda, those two passed away and were reborn there.

Furthermore, Ānanda, all those bodhisattvas who have been reborn in that buddha-field are endowed with the thirty-two marks of a great man, possess perfectly complete limbs, and are skilled in meditation and the superknowledges.

They are skilled in the distinctions of wisdom, possess sharp faculties, have well-restrained senses, possess the faculty of one who has already understood, have undiminished powers of the faculties, have attained patient acceptance, and possess infinite and boundless virtues.

Furthermore, Ānanda, all those bodhisattvas who have been reborn in that buddha-field are never separated from the sight of the Buddha; they are of a nature not to fall into the lower realms until they reach the limit of enlightenment.

From that time forward, all of them shall never again be forgetful of their births, except in the case of such cosmic upheavals as those previously vowed for when the five corruptions prevail; and whenever there is the appearance of Blessed Buddhas in the world, just as there is now for me.
Furthermore, Ānanda, as for those bodhisattvas who have been reborn in that buddha-field,

they all, by means of a single morning meal, travel to other world-systems and attend upon many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddhas, as far as they desire, through the power of the Buddha.

In whatever way they resolve, "May we perform worship with such things as flowers, incense, lamps, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, parasols, banners, flags, victory banners, musical instruments, songs,
and instrumental music," at the very moment those thoughts arise, all such articles for worship appear in their hands.
Performing worship with those flowers and even with musical instruments to those Blessed Buddhas, they accumulate vast, immeasurable, and incalculable merit.

Furthermore, if they should desire, "May such baskets of flowers appear in my hand," then simultaneously with the arising of that thought, divine baskets of flowers— of various colors, many hues, and diverse fragrances— appear in their hands.
With those such flower-baskets, they scatter, shower, and strew them over those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones. And whichever flower-basket,
even the most modest, is released among them, it appears in the sky above as a flower-parasol ten yojanas in width.
And when the second [flower] has not been released, the first does not fall to the ground.
There are flower-baskets there which, once released, appear in the sky above as flower-parasols twenty yojanas in width;
some are thirty, forty, or fifty yojanas in width.
There appeared flower-parasols in the sky above, extending for as many as hundreds of thousands of yojanas;
therein, those who conceived a sublime joy and gladness, and attained a sublime exultation of mind, [were established].
Having planted vast, immeasurable, and incalculable roots of merit, and having served many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddhas,

they once again establish themselves in the world-system Sukhāvatī within a single forenoon, by virtue of the sustaining power of the former vows of that very Tathāgata Amitāyus, through their previous hearing of the Dharma, and because of the roots of merit they had previously planted under former Victors.
By means of a body that has become one with the fulfillment and perfection of former vows, and which is well-proportioned and cultivated.
Furthermore, Ānanda, all those beings who are reborn in that buddha-field speak only such discourses on the Dharma as are accompanied by omniscience.
Furthermore, in that buddha-field, sentient beings have no notion of possession whatsoever.
As they all walk about and move through that buddha-field, they give rise to neither attachment nor aversion;
and as they depart, they do so without longing.

And they do not depart, for they have expectations; indeed, the thought [of departing] does not exist at all in any sentient being there. Furthermore, Ānanda, as for those beings who have been reborn in that world-system Sukhāvatī,
They have no notion of any one among them,
no notion of "self," and no notion of inequality.
There is no quarreling, there is no dispute, and there is no opposition.
They were even-minded, friendly-minded, gentle-minded, affectionate-minded, pliant-minded, serene-minded,

stable-minded, unobstructed-minded, undisturbed-minded, unagitated-minded, and possessed of minds engaged in the practice of the perfection of wisdom; they had entered into the intellect that takes mind as its support,
and were equal to the ocean in wisdom.
Equal to Mount Meru in intelligence,
they are an accumulation of manifold virtues,
sporting in the communal chanting of the factors of enlightenment.
Devoted to the communal recitation of the Buddhas, they investigate with the fleshly eye, manifest the divine eye, and—

having mastered the range of the wisdom-eye and reached the further shore of the Dharma-eye— they bring forth the Buddha-eye; producing, displaying, illuminating, and extensively revealing it, they manifest unimpeded knowledge.

Devoted to the equality of the three realms, they possess tamed minds and peaceful minds; they are endowed with the realization of the entire realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), skilled in the etymological definitions of its arising, and possessed of the etymological definitions of all phenomena. They are skilled in what is to be taken up and what is to be discarded, skilled in the right and wrong methods, and skilled in the proper place;
they dwell without regard for worldly talk.

They realize the essence through supramundane discourses; they are skilled in the investigation of all phenomena, dwelling in the knowledge of the natural quiescence of the nature of all phenomena; their sphere is non-apprehension;
they are without possessions, without grasping, without anxiety, and without substrata; being liberated without clinging, they are stainless and do not remain fixed in any state.

They are firmly established in the supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*), conduct themselves without attachment, and are undaunted; they are devoted to profound dharmas and do not sink back; having ascended into the entry into the Buddha-knowledge that is difficult to awaken to, they have reached the path of the single way (*ekāyanamārga*); they are free from doubt, have crossed over all hesitation, possess knowledge independent of others, and are free from pride.
They have risen high through wisdom like Mount Sumeru;
they are unshakeable in their intelligence like the ocean;
and they surpass the radiance of the moon and sun by virtue of their wisdom and their minds that are white, very bright, pure, and auspicious.
They resemble refined gold by virtue of their radiant luster;
they are like the earth by virtue of their endurance of the good and evil of all sentient beings;
and they are like water by virtue of their flowing stream that washes away the roots of all afflictions.
They are like fire because they burn away the afflictions of conceiving all phenomena;
they are like wind because they do not adhere to any world;
and they are like space because they penetrate all phenomena and are entirely devoid of anything substantial.
They are like lotuses because they are unsullied by all worlds;
they are like great clouds following the rain-season because they roar forth the Dharma;
they are like a great downpour because they rain down the waters of the Dharma.
They are like bulls because they overcome great multitudes;
they are like great elephants because their minds are supremely well-tamed;
they are like noble thoroughbred horses because they are perfectly disciplined.
They are like lions, the kings of beasts, because they are undaunted by their prowess and fearlessness;
they are like the king of Nyagrodha trees, because they provide protection for all sentient beings;
they are like the king of mountains, because they cannot be shaken by any opposing disputants.
They are like the sky because they manifest immeasurable loving-kindness;
they are equal to Great Brahmās because they are preceded by sovereignty over all roots of merit and dharmas;
they are like birds because they do not abide in any accumulation.
They are like the king of birds, the garuḍa, because they shatter all opposing disputants;
they are like the udumbara flower, because they are difficult to encounter and free from adversaries;
and they are like elephants, because they are perfectly concentrated, undistracted, and have upright faculties.
They are skilled in definitive discernment, abundant in patience and gentleness;
they are free from envy because they do not long for the success of others;
they are confident in preaching the Dharma and insatiable in their quest for the Dharma.
They are like beryl in their ethical discipline;
they are mines of jewels in their learning;
and they possess beautiful voices with the resonance of the great drum of the Dharma.

Beating the great drum of the Dharma, blowing the great conch of the Dharma, raising the great banner of the Dharma, and kindling the torch of the Dharma; they are observers with wisdom, undeluded, faultless, with all obstructions stilled, pure, free from the stench of impurity,
without greed, delighting in sharing, liberated in renunciation, open-handed, and devoted to giving both the Dharma and material goods.

In generosity, they are free from stinginess; they are unadulterated, with fearless minds, dispassionate, steadfast, leaders, resolute, modest, possessing well-organized courage, profound, having attained the superknowledges, gentle, pleasant to dwell with, benefactors, and illuminators of the world. Steadfast against misfortune, they have utterly destroyed passion and darkness.

Free from sorrow, stainless, devoid of blinking, sporting with the superknowledges, empowered by the force of causes and the force of vows, straightforward and not crooked— these sons of the Conquerors have planted roots of merit for hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of times; they have uprooted the thorn of pride, are free from passion, hatred, and delusion, pure, possessed of pure resolve, praised by the power of the Conquerors, wise in the world, perfected through refined wisdom, and endowed with a joyful heart.

They are heroes, steadfast, selfless, complete, incomparable, free from passion, harmonious, noble, preeminent, modest, resolute, mindful, wise, and possessed of insight; they have the weapon of wisdom as their armament, are meritorious, radiant, free from all obstructions, rid of impurities, endowed with mindfulness, and have attained the support of peaceful knowledge.
"Ānanda, such are the beings in that buddha-field in brief.
Furthermore, even if the Tathāgata were to describe them with a lifespan lasting for hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of eons,
it would still not be possible to reach the limit of the virtues of those true persons."
And there shall be no interruption of the Tathāgata’s fearlessness.
Why is that?
Because, Ānanda, both of these are inconceivable and incomparable: namely, the virtues of those bodhisattvas and the unsurpassed wisdom and eloquence of the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, Ānanda, arise! Turn toward the west, join your palms scattering flowers, and prostrate yourself.

This is that direction where the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One Amitābha, dwells, remains, and maintains himself, teaching the Dharma— dustless and pure— whose name is proclaimed throughout the unobstructed world in the ten directions; in each direction, Buddhas, Blessed Ones, as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā, repeatedly, again and again, describe, praise, and extol him with unimpeded speech that is beyond reply.

When this had been said, the venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One: "O Blessed One, I desire to see that Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Amitābha, of immeasurable light and immeasurable life, as well as those Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas who have planted roots of merit under many hundreds of thousands of myriads of kotis of Buddhas.
As soon as these words had been spoken by the venerable Ānanda— (Sukhv, Vaidya 248)

Vāk. Then, at that very moment, the Tathāgata Amitābha, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, emitted from the palm of his own hand a ray of light such that this hundred-thousand-koṭi-niyuta-thousandth buddha-field was filled with a great radiance.
Furthermore, at that time, whatever Black Mountains (Kālaparvata) there were throughout all those hundred-thousand-koṭi buddha-fields—
Whether they were mountains of jewels, or Mount Meru, Mahāmeru, Mucilinda, Mahāmucilinda, Cakravāla, or Mahācakravāla;
or whether they were altars, pillars, trees, thickets, groves, or celestial and human palaces—
all of these were completely pierced and overwhelmed by the radiance of that Tathāgata.
Just as a man standing at a distance of one fathom might behold a second man when the sun has risen,

even so, at that very moment, the monks, nuns, laymen, laywomen, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans in this buddha-field beheld that Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Amitābha, like Mount Sumeru.
He saw the king of mountains, which rises above all lands, outshining all directions as it blazes, glows, shines, and radiates;
and he saw that great assembly of bodhisattvas and that community of monks, because of the purity of that light through the power of the Buddha.
It was as if this great earth had become a single expanse of water.
Therein, neither trees, nor mountains, nor islands, nor grasses, shrubs, herbs, or forest giants would be perceived, nor would rivers, chasms, or precipices be known;
rather, the great earth would be a single expanse of one ocean.

Just so, in that buddha-field there is no other mark or sign whatsoever, except for the śrāvakas who possess a fathom-wide radiance, and the bodhisattvas who possess a radiance of hundreds of thousands of millions of leagues.
And that Blessed One, the Tathāgata Amitābha, the Arhat, the Perfectly Awakened One, outshining that assembly of śrāvakas and that assembly of bodhisattvas, was seen illuminating all directions.
At that very time, the bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, gods, and humans in that world-system Sukhāvatī all beheld this Sahā world-system and the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, the Arhat, the Perfectly Awakened One.
They saw him, surrounded by the community of monks, teaching the Dharma.
START Sukhv 40:
Thereupon, the Blessed One addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Ajita: "Ajita, do you see this perfection of the array of qualities and ornaments in that buddha-field?
And do you see above in the sky these delightful parks, delightful gardens, and delightful rivers and lotus ponds, strewn with various jewels and blue, red, yellow, and white lotuses?"

And from the surface of the earth below up to the Akaniṣṭha heaven above, the expanse of space was strewn with flowers, adorned with rows of flower garlands, clearly manifest with rows of pillars made of various jewels, and frequented by various flocks of birds manifested by the Tathāgata?
Ajita the Bodhisattva said: "I see it, Blessed One."

The Blessed One said: "Ajita, do you see these hosts of gods and brahmins making themselves known throughout all the Buddha-fields with the voice of a Buddha, so that these bodhisattvas are never separated from them?
Ajita replied: "I see them, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said: "Furthermore, Ajita, do you see these beings in this Buddha-field, mounted upon celestial palaces a hundred thousand yojanas high, moving through the sky with great honor?"
Ajita said, "I see it, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said, "What do you think, Ajita? Is there any difference between the gods who wield power over the creations of others and the humans in the world-system Sukhāvatī?
Ajita said, "Blessed One, I do not perceive even a single difference, for the humans here in the world-system Sukhāvatī possess such great supernormal powers."
The Blessed One said: "Ajita, do you see those humans in that world-system Sukhāvatī dwelling within their wombs inside magnificent lotuses?

He replied: "It is just as if the Trāyastriṃśa gods or the Yāma gods, having entered celestial palaces fifty yojanas, or a hundred yojanas, or five hundred yojanas in extent, were playing, sporting, and enjoying themselves."
In the same way, Blessed One, I see here in this world-system of Sukhāvatī that these humans dwell within the womb of magnificent lotuses.
START Sukh-v 41:
Furthermore, Blessed One, there are indeed beings here who appear spontaneously upon lotuses in the cross-legged posture.
What, Blessed One, is the cause, what is the condition, that others dwell in the womb?
"But others who are of miraculous birth appear seated cross-legged upon lotuses?

The Blessed One said: "Ajita, those bodhisattvas residing in other buddha-fields who conceive doubt regarding rebirth in the world-system Sukhāvatī, yet plant roots of merit with that very same thought,"

For them, there is residence in a womb here [in this world]. However, those who, having produced freedom from doubt and severed their uncertainty, plant roots of merit for the sake of rebirth in the world-system Sukhāvatī,
and who conceive of, have faith in, and resolve with conviction upon the unimpeded knowledge of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones— [for them, there is no such residence].
They appear spontaneously on lotuses in the cross-legged posture.

Ajita, those bodhisattva mahāsattvas who, while residing in other buddha-fields, give rise to the thought of seeing the Tathāgata Amitābha, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, and do not harbor any doubt— [they too appear there].
They do not doubt the unattached wisdom of a Buddha and have deep faith in their own roots of merit;

for those who appear spontaneously seated in the cross-legged posture, within a mere moment their bodies become such that they are indistinguishable from other beings who have been born there for a long time.
Behold, Ajita, the distinction of wisdom, the diversity of wisdom, the decline of wisdom, and the meagerness of wisdom— namely,
that for five hundred years they have fallen away from seeing the Buddhas, seeing the Bodhisattvas, hearing the Dharma, and discussing the Dharma;
they have fallen away from the practice of the roots of virtue through all the perfections of the roots of virtue, because of their perceptions and mental attentions that have fallen into doubt.

It is just as if, Ajita, there were a prison for an anointed Kṣatriya king, entirely inlaid with gold and beryl; draped with bundles of silk ribbons, garlands, and festoons; with canopies of various colors and splendors; covered with fine cotton cloths and silken bands; strewn with various flowers and blossoms; perfumed with noble incense;
and adorned with palaces, towers, turrets, windows, railings, and archways, all made of the seven jewels and covered by a network of tinkling bells.
It was square, with four pillars, four doors, and four stairways.

Therein, for some reason or other, that son of the king was cast and bound with fetters made of Jāmbūnada gold. And there a couch had been prepared for him, spread with many woolen rugs, covered with cotton mattresses and leaf-mats, provided with a Kāliṅga cloak as a coverlet, with an upper cloth and a bedsheet, and featuring red pillows at both ends, all variegated.
He would be handsome; at that time, he might have sat down or entered there, and much various kinds of pure and refined food and drink would be served to him.
"What do you think, Ajita, would that enjoyment of the prince be magnificent?
Ajita said, "It would be magnificent, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said, "What do you think, Ajita, would he even taste it there and observe it?"
Or would one find satisfaction in that?
He replied: "Certainly not, Blessed One.
On the contrary, even if he were removed from there and cast into a prison by the king,"
He would then desire only liberation;
he would seek out high-born princes, ministers, women of the harem, guild-leaders, householders, and local kings,
so that they might release him from that prison.
Moreover, Blessed One, although that prince finds no delight there in the prison-house,
he is not yet liberated from it as long as the king does not show him favor.

The Blessed One said: "In the same way, Ajita, those bodhisattvas who, having fallen into doubt, nevertheless plant roots of merit and yearn for the Buddha-knowledge— even though it is only by hearing the name of that Buddha and by that mere clarity of mind that they are reborn here in the world-system Sukhāvatī."
However, those born by transformation do not appear upon lotuses in cross-legged postures;
rather, they dwell within the womb-like interior of the lotuses. Furthermore, although they maintain the perception of gardens and celestial palaces there, [they do not actually exist].
There is no excrement or urine, no saliva or mucus, and nothing disagreeable arises for the mind.

Furthermore, for five hundred years they shall be deprived of the sight of the Buddha, the hearing of the Dharma, the sight of Bodhisattvas, the definitive discussion of the Dharma, all roots of merit, and the practice of the Dharma;
although they do not take delight therein, nor do they experience satisfaction.
Moreover, indeed, they will exhaust their previous and subsequent [lifetimes] and only afterwards emerge;
yet, as they emerge from there, no emergence is perceived—whether upwards, downwards, or across.

Behold, Ajita, how now, after five hundred years, there shall be many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of services rendered to Buddhas, and many immeasurable, incalculable, and unfathomable roots of merit to be planted.
They destroy all of that through the fault of doubt.
Behold, Ajita, how great a calamity doubt brings about for bodhisattvas!
Therefore, Ajita, bodhisattvas should, free from doubt, generate the mind set on awakening in order to swiftly establish the welfare and happiness of all sentient beings.

In order to attain capability and for the sake of rebirth in the world-system of Sukhāvatī, where the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, Arhat, and Perfectly Enlightened Buddha Amitābha resides, one should dedicate one's roots of merit.

START Sukhv 42: When this had been said, the Bodhisattva Ajita addressed the Blessed One as follows: "Furthermore, Blessed One, will Bodhisattvas who have reached perfection in this Buddha-field, or those from the presence of other Blessed Buddhas, be reborn in the world-system Sukhāvatī?"

The Blessed One said: "Ajita, from this buddha-field, seventy-two billion *koṭī-niyuta*s of perfected bodhisattvas will be reborn in the world-system Sukhāvatī—those who have planted roots of merit under many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddhas and are perfected non-retrogressing ones.

What need is there to mention those with even more limited roots of merit? From the presence of the Tathāgata Duṣprasaha, eighteen hundred billion *koṭī-niyuta*s of bodhisattvas will be reborn in the world-system Sukhāvatī."
In the eastern direction, there dwells a Tathāgata named Ratnākara;
from his presence, ninety koṭis of bodhisattvas will be reborn in the world-system Sukhāvatī.
From the presence of the Tathāgata Jyotiṣprabha, twenty-two koṭis of bodhisattvas will be reborn in the world-system Sukhāvatī.
Twenty-five koṭis of bodhisattvas will be reborn in the world-system Sukhāvatī from the presence of the Tathāgata Amitaprabha;
sixty koṭis of bodhisattvas will be reborn in the world-system Sukhāvatī from the presence of the Tathāgata Lokapradīpa;
and sixty-four koṭis of bodhisattvas will be reborn in the world-system Sukhāvatī from the presence of the Tathāgata Nāgābhibhū.
Twenty-five koṭis of bodhisattvas will be reborn in the world-system Sukhāvatī from the presence of the Tathāgata Virajaprabha.
Sixteen koṭis of bodhisattvas will be reborn in the world-system Sukhāvatī from the presence of the Tathāgata Siṃha.
Eighteen thousand bodhisattvas will be reborn in the world-system Sukhāvatī from the presence of the Tathāgata Siṃha.
From the presence of the Tathāgata Śrīkūṭa, eighty-one koṭī-niyutas of bodhisattvas will be reborn in the world-system Sukhāvatī.
From the presence of the Tathāgata Narendrarāja, ten koṭī-niyutas of bodhisattvas will be reborn in the world-system Sukhāvatī.
From the presence of the Tathāgata Balābhijña, twelve thousand bodhisattvas will be reborn in the world-system Sukhāvatī.
From the presence of the Tathāgata Puṣpadhvaja, twenty-five koṭis of bodhisattvas who have attained vigor set out on a single journey;
within a single eight-day period, they will turn back ninety-nine quadrillion kalpas and be reborn in the world-system Sukhāvatī.
From the presence of the Tathāgata Jvalanādhipati, twelve koṭis of bodhisattvas will be reborn in the world-system Sukhāvatī;
from the presence of the Tathāgata Vaiśāradyaprāpta, sixty-nine koṭis of bodhisattvas will be reborn in the world-system Sukhāvatī,
in order to behold, pay homage to, attend upon, question, and interrogate the Tathāgata Amitābha.

In this manner, Ajita, for a full hundred thousand million billion eons, I could proclaim the names of those Tathāgatas from whom those bodhisattvas approach in order to see, pay homage to, and attend upon that Tathāgata Amitābha in the world-system Sukhāvatī.
And it is not possible to reach its limit.
START Sukh 43:
Behold, Ajita, how much gain those beings have truly obtained who shall hear the name of the Tathāgata Amitābha, the Arhat, the Perfectly Awakened One!
Nor will those beings be of inferior resolve who express even a single thought of serene faith toward that Tathāgata.
And regarding this Dharma discourse:
therefore, Ajita, I announce to you and declare before the world with its gods that you must listen to this Dharma discourse.
Even having plunged into a trichiliocosm world-system filled with fire, one must not turn back even for the duration of a single thought-moment.
Why is that?
Ajita, it is because millions of bodhisattvas, by not hearing such Dharma-discourses as these, turn away from unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.

Therefore, for the sake of hearing, taking up, retaining, mastering, fully comprehending, extensively proclaiming, and cultivating this Dharma-discourse with a resolute intention, one must exert very great vigor—
even for as little as a single night and day, or even for the duration of a single milking of a cow.
At the very least, having transcribed it into a book, it should be well-written and preserved;

and one who wishes to quickly establish immeasurable beings in the state of non-retrogression regarding unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, and to behold that buddha-field of the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Amitābha, should conceive of that preceptor as the Teacher himself.
And it is in order to acquire for themselves a distinguished excellence of the array of ornaments and qualities of a Buddha-field.

Furthermore, Ajita, those beings who, even when the true Dharma is in the process of vanishing in the future, will encounter such sublime discourses on the Dharma as these, will have most excellently obtained their gain; they will have planted roots of merit, performed services under previous Victors, and be sustained by the empowerment of the Buddhas.

Praised by all Buddhas, extolled by all Buddhas, and authorized by all Buddhas, they will swiftly bring about the attainment of the great knowledge of omniscience and come within the range of hearing.
Having heard them, those who obtain vast joy and rapture will take them up, preserve them, recite them, master them, and reveal them extensively to others.
They will delight in meditative cultivation, and even by merely writing it down, they will worship it;
they will produce great merit.
"It is not easy to calculate its number.
Thus, Ajita, whatever was to be done by the Tathāgata has been done by me;
you must now apply yourselves to being free from doubt."
Do not have any doubt regarding the unattached and unobstructed wisdom of a Buddha;
let there not be an entry into the prison made of jewels planted in every form.
For the appearance of a Buddha, Ajita, is difficult to encounter.
The teaching of the Dharma is difficult to encounter;
the perfection of the opportune moment is difficult to encounter.
And, Ajita, I have proclaimed the attainment of the perfections of all roots of virtue.
Now you must apply yourselves and practice!
Indeed, Ajita, I entrust this Dharma discourse to you with great care.
You shall exert yourselves so that the Buddha-dharmas are not lost and do not disappear.
Do not violate the command of the Tathāgata.
START Sukhv 44:
(Sukhv, Vaidya 252) Then, at that time, the Blessed One spoke these verses:
Such sounds as these shall not reach those who have not performed meritorious deeds;
but those heroes, O Śūra, who have accomplished their goals, shall hear this speech.
For by those who have seen the Perfectly Awakened One, the Lord of the World, the Illuminator—
When the Dharma is heard with reverence, you will attain supreme joy.
Those who are inferior and possessed of indolent views are not able to find faith in the teachings of the Buddhas;
whereas those who have performed worship in the Buddha-fields and trained in the conduct of the Lords of the Three Worlds [are able].
Just as a man who is blind in the darkness does not know the path, how could he show it?
In the same way, the śrāvakas are ignorant of the Buddha’s wisdom; how much more so, then, are sentient beings today?
For a Buddha alone understands the qualities of a Buddha, not gods, nāgas, asuras, yakṣas, or śrāvakas;
for even many Buddhas do not reach the extent of a Buddha’s wisdom when it is being revealed.

If all sentient beings were equal, being experts in ultimate reality and possessing pure wisdom, they might for ten million eons or even longer describe the virtues of a single Buddha. // Sukhv_vs_54 //
In this interval, they may remain in a state of bliss, manifesting for many millions of eons;
yet no measure of the Buddha’s wisdom can be found, for such is the marvelous nature of the Jinas’ knowledge.

Therefore, a wise man of discerning nature who places his trust in my words shall proclaim these utterances, knowing them to be the complete path to the knowledge of the Jina, spoken by a Buddha. (Sukhāvativyūha 56)
Human birth is obtained only at rare intervals; the appearance of Buddhas likewise occurs only at rare intervals.
Faith, purpose, and wisdom are attained only after a very long time; therefore, one should generate vigor for the sake of attaining that goal.

Those who, having heard such a sublime Dharma, obtain joy while recollecting the Sugata, and those who likewise generate the aspiration for enlightenment— they were our friends in the past, and they shall be so in the future.
Thus [it is said]. (Sukhāvativyūha 44)
START Sukhv 45:
Furthermore, while this Dharma discourse was being spoken, the dust-free and stainless Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena was purified for twelve hundred billion beings;
and four hundred quintillion beings attained the fruit.
The minds of eight hundred bhikṣus were liberated from the outflows through non-clinging;
twenty-five koṭis of bodhisattvas attained the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena;
and among the host of gods and humans, four hundred thousand koṭis of niyutas of beings gave rise to the resolve for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment—a resolve never before arisen.
And they have planted roots of merit for rebirth in the world-system Sukhāvatī out of a desire to behold the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Amitābha.
Having all been reborn there, they will gradually become Tathāgatas named Mañjusvara and be reborn in other world-systems.

Furthermore, eighty *niyuta-koṭis* [of beings] who attained patient endurance (*kṣānti*) under the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara shall become non-retrogressive regarding unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, just like Amitāyus himself.
Having been ripened by the Tathāgata while practicing the conduct of a bodhisattva in the past, they will be reborn in the world-system of Sukhāvatī and will fulfill their former vows and practices.
At that moment, this trichiliocosm shook in six ways,
and various miraculous manifestations appeared.
On the earth, refined speech was produced;
divine and human musical instruments resounded;
and by the sound of rejoicing, the entire realm as far as the Akaniṣṭha heaven was made known.
Thus spoke the Blessed One,
and the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Ajita, the Venerable Ānanda, and the entire assembly— including the world of gods, humans, asuras, garuḍas, and gandharvas— rejoiced in what the Blessed One had said.

The Mahāyāna sūtra titled "The Array of Sukhāvatī," the chapter on Amitābha, which proclaims the praises of the qualities of the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Amitābha’s Sukhāvatī, and describes the entry of bodhisattvas into the stage of non-retrogression, is hereby completed.
*All phenomena arise from causes; the Tathāgata has taught their cause.*
And their cessation—such is the teaching of the Great Śramaṇa.
